title: A Patient-Specific Digital Twin for Hydrocephalus Shunts
summary: What if every ventriculoperitoneal shunt came with a simulation of the patient it was going into?
concept: Shunts for normal pressure hydrocephalus are usually set using population-level guidance, yet the risk of over-drainage, and with it subdural hematoma, depends on each patient's anatomy, brain stiffness and posture.

The idea: build a lightweight fluid-structure interaction 'digital twin' from a patient's routine MRI. It would estimate how cerebrospinal fluid drainage reshapes the brain and stresses bridging veins at different valve settings, then suggest the setting with the lowest predicted risk.
Over time, outcomes from real patients would recalibrate the model, turning a one-off simulation into a learning system that gets safer with every case.
questions: Which imaging features are the minimum needed to make the model personal enough to matter?
Can a reduced-order model run fast enough to be used during a clinic visit?
How should clinicians see uncertainty, so the tool supports their judgment instead of replacing it?

title: Self-Reporting Hardware for Reusable Rockets
summary: Reusable boosters fly again and again. Their parts should be able to tell us how much life they have left.
concept: Today, deciding whether a returned booster can fly again relies heavily on inspection. Additively manufactured parts, such as nozzle cooling channels, make this harder because their internal geometry is difficult to inspect.

The idea: design each critical part together with its own sparse sensor layout and a physics-informed prognostic model. During every flight, a handful of strain and temperature readings update a Bayesian estimate of accumulated fatigue damage, with honest uncertainty bands.
The result would be a 'remaining flights' gauge for each component, so refurbishment decisions are driven by evidence rather than conservative fixed limits.
questions: Where should a small number of sensors go to make internal damage observable?
How can flight data from one vehicle improve predictions for the whole fleet?
What level of confidence should be required before extending a part's certified life?

title: Factories That Detect, Decide and Heal
summary: Combining autonomous quality inspection with self-healing materials could close the loop from defect to repair.
concept: Quality inspection and repair are usually separate steps: a defect is found, logged and fixed later, often by a person. Self-healing polymer composites raise a different possibility: parts that can repair some damage themselves when triggered.

The idea: connect an autonomous quality intelligence system directly to self-healing materials. When sensors or vision detect micro-damage, the system decides whether the damage is within the healable range, triggers the repair (for example with local heat), and then re-inspects to confirm it worked.
Every cycle becomes training data, teaching the factory which defects can be healed in place and which need a human expert.
questions: Which damage types are reliably healable, and how do we verify the repair is structurally sound?
How should the decision logic balance speed, cost and safety?
What new standards would certify a part that has repaired itself?
